headline: Bond Revolt and Hormuz Anxiety Cloud Tuesday's Open
body_html:
Tuesday's pre-market tone is defensive. Escalating tensions in the Strait of Hormuz — where a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile over the weekend, killing at least one crew member — have rattled fixed-income and commodity markets overnight. The 30-year Treasury yield has climbed to its highest level since 2007, a 19-year peak, as bond investors reassess risk amid an expiring U.S.-Iran ceasefire and the prospect of a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most critical shipping chokepoints. The dollar is soft as expectations for near-term Federal Reserve rate hikes fade, but that relief is being more than offset by the anxiety rippling through bond markets.

Oil is holding near a three-week high above $91 as hopes for a diplomatic resolution dim, adding cost pressure across consumer and industrial sectors. Gold, meanwhile, is slipping as firmer Treasury yields and elevated oil prices compete for safe-haven flows. Investors will be watching the Federal Reserve's July meeting minutes — due later today — for any recalibration signals on the rate path.

Monday's session offered a preview of the day's fault lines: semiconductors outperformed sharply, gaining 1.71%, while software shed 1.90% and consumer names fell 1.38%. Breadth was clearly negative, with 345 names declining against 202 advancing across our 550-name universe. Expect that bifurcation to remain a feature at Tuesday's open as macro headwinds dominate the tape.

briefs.headline: 30-Year Treasury Yield Reaches a 19-Year High
briefs.body: The long end of the U.S. yield curve has pushed to levels unseen since 2007, rattled by geopolitical risk and fading confidence in a swift Middle East resolution. Analysts identify three potential catalysts that could drive yields even higher: a formal Hormuz blockade, a broader regional escalation, and a hawkish pivot in Fed communications.

briefs.headline: Hormuz Shipping Data Remains Critically Thin
briefs.body: Vessel crossings through the Strait of Hormuz edged up only marginally from the weekend but remain in single digits, according to tracking data — a fraction of normal traffic. A projectile strike on a commercial vessel, with at least one crew casualty confirmed by the UK Maritime Trade Operations, has deepened the crisis and kept shipping insurers on high alert.

briefs.headline: argenx Surges More Than 16% to Lead Monday's Gainers
briefs.body: Biotech firm argenx posted the session's biggest gain, climbing 16.04% in Monday's trading. The move stood out sharply in an otherwise broadly negative tape, suggesting company-specific news drove the advance. The stock's sector — healthcare-biotech — otherwise saw mixed results as the broader healthcare group dipped 0.17%.

briefs.headline: Semiconductor Names Defy the Selloff With Broad Gains
briefs.body: The semiconductor sector rose 1.71% on Monday, the only major group to post a meaningful advance. Semtech jumped nearly 10%, Sandisk gained 8.88%, and Credo Technology added 8.82%, while optical networking name Coherent rose 7.79%. The cluster of gains points to sustained demand expectations despite a softening macro backdrop.

briefs.headline: China Returns to Oil Stockpiling, Quietly Reshaping Crude Flows
briefs.body: Beijing surprised markets in July by resuming oil stockpiling after a period of restraint, according to new trade data. Separately, China's refined fuel exports are edging back toward pre-conflict levels as regulators ease export curbs. The dual development complicates the global oil supply picture at a moment when Hormuz disruptions are already tightening physical markets.

briefs.headline: Software and Consumer Stocks Bear the Brunt of Monday's Retreat
briefs.body: Software names fell 1.90% as a group Monday, the session's worst-performing sector, while consumer stocks dropped 1.38%. ZoomInfo shed 7.16%, H&R Block tumbled 7.03%, and apparel retailer Victoria's Secret lost 5.53%. The weakness reflects broad pressure on discretionary and growth-oriented names as long-dated yields climb and risk appetite contracts.
